summary.text:
Havering's Annual Treasury Management Report 2025/26 to Audit Committee on 30 June 2026 is a compact, well-laid-out paper with all the tables it needs and — unusually — a rate-and-duration column on the detailed maturity table at Appendix A p14 that most councils omit. The reconciliation ties to the pound: 31 PWLB loans, £623,095,573 at 3.4902% weighted, matches Table 1's PWLB row of £623.096m and paragraph 2.6's year-end 3.49% average. The all-in book of £630.974m adds a £7m LOBO with Danske Bank at 3.60% and £0.878m of short-term borrowing.

The shape is a heavy front-end. £354.1m — 56.13% of the debt portfolio — reprices inside two years: £166.6m under 12 months at an average 3.84%, and £187.5m in the 12-24 month bucket at an average 4.10%. The 12-24 month bucket carries the £320m of HRA borrowing taken between February and March 2026 at 4.07% to refinance in-year maturing debt of £297m. Explicit strategy at p5 is 'keeping loan duration short and only borrowing when liquidity requires it'; paragraph 2.5 flags that this 'increases interest rate volatility and will require reassessment during 2026/27'.

The forward path in Appendix A Table 4 is striking: external debt is projected to move from £631m to £1,354m by 31 March 2029 as the CFR moves from £810m to £1,498m. That is £723m of net new drawings to time, on top of rolling the £354m already inside the two-year window. On the other side of the book, the £105m at 1.53% out to 2069-71 (Appendix A p14) is the largest single ultra-cheap legacy tranche we have read in a London borough this cycle, and is what pulls the all-in weighted rate down to 3.49%.

Two small internal notes recorded but kept out of the email: paragraph 6.2 narrative gives CFR as £806m against Table 2's £810m — £4m rounding gap; and the paper computes internal borrowing as CFR minus external debt only (£179m), not netting the £9m OLTL from Appendix A Table 5. Neither is a mistake and neither is the kind of point that can be raised without reading as pedantic. Email drafted around the reconciliation, the £354m two-year refi lump, the CFR forward path, and the £105m at 1.53% as descriptive context.

officer.body:
Hi Tony,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the annual review that went to Audit Committee on 30 June, ahead of the mid-year update in November. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your paper is one of the tidier annual reviews we've read this cycle — the rate-and-duration column on the Appendix A p14 maturity table is something most councils don't publish, and it makes the whole book legible in one page.

A cross-check first. We hold 31 PWLB loans for Havering at 31 March, £623,095,573, weighted 3.4902%. Your Table 1 PWLB row prints £623.096m and paragraph 2.6 gives the year-end average as 3.49% — same book, to the pound and to two decimal places. The all-in £630.974m in Appendix A adds the £7m Danske LOBO and the £0.878m of short-term borrowing, and the maturity buckets tie back with only those small residuals in them.

On that footing the shape that stands out is the front end. £354m — 56% of the debt portfolio — reprices inside two years: £166.6m in the twelve months to March at an average 3.84%, and £187.5m in the year after at 4.10%. £320m of that £354m is the HRA money drawn between February and March at 4.07%, which was well timed against today's certainty rates of 4.95% at one year and 5.06% at two years. It's the rollover of that block in 2027 and 2028 that carries the interest-rate exposure your paragraph 2.5 flags for reassessment during 2026/27.

The forward path in Appendix A Table 4 is the other line worth reading alongside it. External debt is projected to move from £631m to £1,354m by 31 March 2029 as the CFR moves from £810m to £1,498m. That is £723m of net new drawings to time over three years, on top of rolling the £354m already inside the two-year window. It's a lot of borrowing to place against a curve whose long end is 0.11-0.19 higher than 31 March.

The other thing that caught the eye is the £105m at 1.53% out to 2069-71 — 16.6% of the debt portfolio at a rate the sector will not see again, and the largest single ultra-cheap tranche we have read in a London borough this cycle. It's what pulls your all-in average down to 3.49% against the 4.10% currently paid on the 12-24 month bucket, and paragraph 2.9 is right that rescheduling that tranche doesn't work: giving up a 1.53% coupon to replace it at today's rates would cost more than any principal discount could save. We price it daily anyway, at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis — indicative only, only the DMO can quote, and no MRP or accounting treatment is modelled — because for the shorter-dated loans in your book the arithmetic can shift in either direction as the curve moves.

The monthly sector picture is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity — July was £368m across 33 loans from 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%, which is what appetite looks like at these levels before rolling. Rates at both fixings are at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard.

On training, three fit Havering: Strategic PWLB borrowing, for the £354m rolling inside two years and the £723m of net new drawings to place over the three years after; HRA borrowing and the certainty rate, given the HRA has been the source of the recent £320m; and our liability benchmark pathway, which is interactive and built on live data — worth a look given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes. For members, Audit Committee Chair (Treasury) is written for exactly the scrutiny this report gets. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
